What kind of rads, run backwards on the problem.

Confirm whether all rads are running on one line, likely a 3/4 Pex or 1 Inch black iron depending on the size of the house. Or separate lines going to different parts of the house. Remember that at the boiler, you could have multiple applications for the heated water. You may need to follow the lines to see where they're going if they aren't appropriately labeled.

With that information, confirm if you have a particular "loop" that's down, or if you are getting airlocked at a specific rad. While doing that, I'd look at the quality of build relating to your heating system. An example of a red flag is when someone uses the flexibility of Pex to run it through tight spaces, instead of cutting, and fitting 90s into place where appropriate to allow as unimpeded a flow as possible. If it looks sketchy, research further. Is the Pex used an "Oxygen Barrier" brand, or did the do-it-yourselfer who installed it not know the significance and therefore bought the cheapest on the shelf. A non oxygen barrier Pex over time will actually absorb oxygen into the water which in turn will not only corrode the interior components of the boiler to death, it can potentially cause air locks.

Once we know where the problem is specifically in the system, we can attempt to address the airlock. I'd start with bleeders on the rads that encompass the loop were dealing with. All rads have them, normally a flat head, ideally a Thermostat screwdriver is all you need to turn them, have a bucket at the ready, this step requires planning. Find the bleeder, measure it from the ground, and realize you need to find a container that is both low enough to be placed under said bleeder, and still large enough to prevent 100 trips emptying it.

Once you're ready, start bleeding on the first rad on your loop. You can hear air exiting a rad. Pay attention to the change in pitch. Air fractures the consistancy of the sound created from the water exiting. Everytime you hear that distortion, it's more air leaving your system.

Do every rad like this. Once finished, do it again to test if you get anymore air. If there's any, repeat this process. Let's quickly discuss the integral importance of understanding the definition of insanity. If you've been bleeding for 30 - 45 minutes, and it's still airlocking, we have to then figure out what's causing a rapid allowance of air into your system. These systems when functioning correctly are full of "dead water" a closed loop that doesn't accept new water or oxygen, it just continually cycles the water, or sometimes glycol mixture until some kind of intervention ( a service or potential leak) causes a change.
